title: RUP Pesticide Records After the 2025 Federal Change: What Private Applicators Still Need
excerpt: USDA's federal restricted-use pesticide recordkeeping rule ended on July 11, 2025. Here is what changed, what still applies through your state, the label and the Worker Protection Standard, and how to keep records inspection-ready.
author: FarmVoice Records

sections.heading: What changed in 2025?
sections.body: Until 2025, a USDA regulation (7 CFR Part 110) required certified private applicators to keep records of every restricted-use pesticide (RUP) application. USDA removed that regulation effective July 11, 2025, saying the federal program had been unfunded since the early 2010s. The federal two-year recordkeeping rule therefore no longer applies on its own.

sections.heading: What still applies?
sections.body: State pesticide laws, which often require RUP or general-use records of their own, still apply, and the product label is still the law. Farms with agricultural employees must follow the EPA Worker Protection Standard, which has its own requirements for application information. Your state department of agriculture or extension service can tell you exactly what applies to your operation.

sections.heading: What should a good RUP record include?
sections.body: The former federal list is still a sound checklist: the brand name and EPA registration number, the total amount applied, the location and size of the area treated, the crop, commodity or site, the date, and the certified applicator's name and certification number. Recording these within a day or two of each application, while details are fresh, keeps records accurate.

sections.heading: How long should you keep records?
sections.body: Follow your state's retention period; where none applies, keeping records for at least two to three years is a common, conservative practice. Incomplete or missing records make inspections, insurance claims, neighbor disputes and worker-protection questions much harder to resolve.

sections.heading: Check your state's rules
sections.body: Requirements differ by state: some require use reports, some require records for general-use products too, and retention periods vary. Always confirm the current rules with your state department of agriculture or extension service rather than relying on a general article.

sections.heading: How FarmVoice Records helps
